name: Fenwick binary indexed tree prefix sums
definition: For 1≤i≤n, let b(i)=2^{v_2(i)} and T_i=Σ_{j=i−b(i)+1}^i x_j. Prefix P(k)=Σ_{j=1}^k x_j is obtained from sum=0 by adding T_i for i=k,k−b(k),… until i=0. For a point increment x_k←x_k+δ, add δ to T_i for i=k,k+b(k),… while i≤n.
variables: n positive integer array length; i,k one-based indices except prefix k=0; v_2(i) exponent of the largest power of two dividing i; b(i) that power; T_i block sum; δ additive increment
assumptions: Fixed n≥1, exact commutative additive arithmetic with zero; prefix index 0≤k≤n and update index 1≤k≤n; enough integer width for indices and arithmetic; signed values and increments allowed for sums only
limitations: O(n) stored sums and O(1+log n) additions per query or point increment. Initialization by n updates costs O(n log(n+1)). Finite-precision addition may round or overflow. Prefix search by cumulative rank and arbitrary range updates are not part of this specification
failure_conditions: Reject noninteger or out-of-range index, especially zero for an update
Reject unsupported arithmetic or potential index/value overflow
computation: Initialize all T_i to zero and insert each initial value with the point-increment rule. For a prefix use a zero accumulator and subtract b(i) from each positive index. For increment, visit the increasing chain of covering blocks; stop once the next index exceeds n. If additive inverses exist, interval sum on [l,r] is P(r)−P(l−1).

source.citation: Fenwick (1994), A new data structure for cumulative frequency tables, Software: Practice and Experience 24(3), 327–336, Principles and Figures 4–5, pp. 328–331; DOI 10.1002/spe.4380240306. https://www.plouffe.fr/OEIS/archive_in_pdf/spe884.pdf

application: General mutable prefix sums; no empirical benefit claimed.
required_inputs: Array size, values and indexed additive updates.
incompatible_methods: Using zero index in the one-based update
mechanism_note: Subtracting the lowest set bit partitions the prefix into disjoint consecutive dyadic intervals; adding that bit enumerates precisely the stored intervals containing the changed index. The update increases the lowest set-bit size until leaving the array. This is the one-based positive-index form with no stored index-zero frequency, unlike the paper's special zero slot. Distinct mutable dyadic representation, not chronological bucket coalescence or static pairwise summation.

name: Segment tree associative range aggregate
definition: For a nonempty array indexed 1,…,n, A(l,l)=x_l and A(l,r)=A(l,m)⊗A(m+1,r) for m=⌊(l+r)/2⌋ when l<r. Query Q(l,r;a,b)=e if [l,r]∩[a,b] is empty, A(l,r) if [l,r]⊆[a,b], otherwise Q(l,m;a,b)⊗Q(m+1,r;a,b).
variables: n positive integer length; l,r inclusive node endpoints; m split; a,b inclusive query endpoints; ⊗ associative operation; e two-sided identity; A stored ordered aggregate; Q range query
assumptions: Fixed n≥1; values in a monoid (closed associative operation with two-sided identity); valid nonempty query 1≤a≤b≤n or explicitly empty query returning e; exact operation for mathematical equality
limitations: O(n) aggregate slots and build combines; O(1+log n) combines for a point replacement or contiguous range query. Time bounds assume constant-cost combine and storage per aggregate. Floating-point nonassociativity, overflow, or growing aggregate sizes can invalidate exact or constant-cost claims. No lazy range updates or dynamic resizing here
failure_conditions: Reject invalid nonempty query or replacement index
Reject nonassociative operation, incorrect identity, or arithmetic overflow
computation: Build on the actual inclusive interval without padding, stopping at singleton leaves. On query return the identity for a disjoint node and the stored value for a fully included node; otherwise recurse on left and right in that order. For replacement set the corresponding leaf and recompute each ancestor left-to-right. An explicitly empty query returns e without traversal.

source.citation: Carnegie Mellon University, 15-451 Algorithm Design and Analysis, Fall 2024, Range query data structures, sections 2–3 and 5.1, pp. 3–7 and 8–9. https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15451-f24/lectures/lecture06-range-queries.pdf

application: General mutable range aggregation; no empirical benefit claimed.
incompatible_methods: Reordering operands for a noncommutative operation
mechanism_note: Induction on interval splits proves every node stores the ordered fold, and disjoint query pieces concatenate in original order. Only the two boundary paths can contain partially intersecting nodes at each depth, yielding logarithmic combine count. Unlike Fenwick prefix differences, arbitrary monoid ranges require no inverse or commutativity. This is the independently derived unpadded inclusive formulation of the course's balanced half-open tree, not a new entry for each aggregate.
